Ukraine has shared the names of more than half a million Russian soldiers, but fewer than 1% have been added to the EU’s Schengen security database. Brussels is now exploring ways to overcome the legal hurdles amid growing concerns over Russian security threats.

EU countries are struggling to keep Russian soldiers and war veterans out of Europe because of legal and bureaucratic obstacles that have prevented them from adding hundreds of thousands of names to the bloc's shared security database.

Ukraine has supplied European authorities with the identities of more than half a million Russian soldiers, amid growing fears that combatants returning from the frontline could pose a security threat.

But after almost a year of work, EU countries have managed to enter fewer than 1% of those names into the Schengen Information System (SIS), which border guards use to identify people who should be refused entry.

Ukraine has been compiling a database of Russian soldiers identified on the frontline and systematically sharing it with Estonia. Tallinn, in turn, passes the information to countries including Germany, Lithuania, Poland and Czechia.

In recent months, officials in these countries have been painstakingly entering the names into SIS, the EU's main shared database for security, border management and law enforcement.

Border guards routinely consult it when checking travellers at the external borders, and police can use it for law-enforcement purposes.

Originally conceived as a security measure to compensate for the abolition of internal border controls within the Schengen area, the system has gradually expanded to cover a much broader range of security and migration alerts.

There is, however, a practical and legal obstacle. SIS was not designed as a mass watchlist of foreign military personnel who have never set foot in Europe. Its legal framework requires authorities to establish specific grounds for each alert, including an individual assessment of the threat a person poses.

As a result, countries trying to keep Russian combatants out have had to work within a system built around individual alerts and decisions, not a blanket mechanism for flagging entire categories of foreign nationals.

Individual assessments

Kyiv typically shares information identifying Russian soldiers and their alleged involvement in the war, along with details such as their location on the frontline. That does not automatically meet the legal bar for an SIS entry.

Under EU rules on SIS alerts for refusal of entry and stay, national authorities must carry out an individual assessment and establish that the person’s presence would threaten public policy, public security or national security.

This means authorities cannot simply upload Ukraine’s database into SIS. They must gather and assess further information on each person, establish the legal grounds and take a formal decision before issuing an alert. The process is lengthy and resource-intensive, especially for a database of hundreds of thousands of names.

Given the high death toll among Russian troops on the frontline, some of those listed may already be dead. Despite these inefficiencies, national authorities have been left with no better option.

“At this stage, we have nothing better to do than put these people in the SIS; it’s the most effective system,” an EU diplomat told Euronews, noting that when one member state enters a name, the alert becomes binding on all the others.

It is not the first time national authorities have run into this problem. A very similar case arose with former ISIS members, but those numbered a few hundred, not hundreds of thousands.

Ban on combatants

EU institutions and governments have therefore spent recent months discussing technical ways to bar current and former Russian combatants from European soil.

The issue was a sticking point in negotiations on the latest sanctions package against Russia, adopted in July, and was watered down at the insistence of Italy and France.

Under the final compromise, the package does not apply the combatants ban directly but makes it conditional on implementing measures. The Commission is working on them and could present them as early as the next Foreign Affairs Council on 16 November.

Meanwhile, Russia’s hybrid threats have become increasingly physical. The most prominent case is the attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport in August, which Berlin formally attributed to Moscow in September.

Shifting security landscape

The episode has shifted perceptions of the Russian threat across Europe. Northern and eastern European countries are pushing to restrict tourist visas for Russians, while the likes of Italy, France and Spain issue them in large numbers.

At an informal ministerial meeting in early September, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said there was “broad support” for moving forward with a ban on tourist visas for Russian soldiers and war veterans.

“The moment you say it was Russia, you need to react, or you are inviting more attacks. France understands this and has moved; it is only Italy standing in the way now,” a second EU diplomat told Euronews on condition of anonymity.

While France’s position appears to have shifted, Italy remains sceptical, fearing its consular services would be overloaded identifying Russian ex-combatants among visa applicants, as well as potential legal challenges.

Rome, however, faces an awkward fact: one of the main suspects in the Leipzig attempted attack was a Belarusian citizen who entered the EU on a tourist visa issued by the Italian consulate in Minsk. The other was a Russian-born Latvian citizen.

Political opposition seems to be gradually giving way, but the question remains technical and, above all, legal. EU officials fear a flood of court challenges, which makes finding a solid solution all the more pressing.

Technical solutions

The EU delegation in Moscow initially held several rounds of consultations with member states' consulates on operational challenges. But consular procedures are not the main obstacle, and arrangements are expected to be put in place relatively quickly.

A Commission paper circulated during the last sanctions negotiations, seen by Euronews, proposed expanding the list of supporting documents Russians must submit for an EU visa to include military booklets for men of conscription age.

Officials also worry about circumvention: Russian authorities might systematically forge the booklets or even supply entirely false identities. That is why certain EU countries, like Czechia, only allow Russians with biometric passports to enter.

“The question is not so much whether we will respond or not but if the measure will be solid or not,” an EU official with direct knowledge of the matter told Euronews. “We need to put a system in place, but we also need to make sure it cannot be circumvented.”

A longer-term fix would be to amend the Schengen Borders Code, giving member states more flexibility in managing SIS and moving from individual listings to a new category covering people believed to pose a security threat.

This could be paired with a revision of the Visa Code, which the Commission is expected to propose in early 2027, giving the EU the power to adopt coordinated restrictions on specific categories of travellers, including combatants from an aggressor state.

Diplomatic restrictions

A separate track concerns further limits on the movement of Russian diplomatic and consular staff, also seen as a security liability amid escalating hybrid attacks.

The 19th sanctions package already restricted Russian diplomats’ movement by requiring them to notify authorities in a second member state before travelling to or transiting through it.

But while advance notification is mandatory, an optional mechanism requiring diplomats to obtain prior authorisation has largely gone unused.

Across these initiatives, the EU faces the same challenge: finding a practical, legally sound solution that preserves a coordinated European approach while delivering a firm response to Russia's hybrid threats.

The EU's CBAM took effect in January 2026, covering imports of aluminum, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, iron and steel, effectively obliging operators to pay for the CO2 emissions linked to their production.

Shortly after its launch, several EU countries sought temporarily exemptions for fertilisers, warning that the tax would push up prices and could undermine food security. Their request was ultimately not conceded by the European Commission.

Brussels argues that CBAM prevents EU manufacturers from being undercut by imports produced under weaker climate rules. However, developing economies counter that it is an unfair practice, describing it as a unilateral measure that could penalise their industries and restrict their development. While foreign players don't need to pay for their emissions, they need to comply with monitoring and reporting, which they argue is too burdensome.

Piyush Goyal, India's commerce minister, recently attacked the economic consequences of CBAM at the Berlin Global Dialogue.

“If you have put a CBAM on yourself, you put a 50% import duty to bring steel into your country, you are inviting disaster. Your cost of living will go up. Your people will be unhappy. Your industry will be out-priced," said Goyal.

The timing is significant. Brussels is negotiating plans to extend CBAM to more products, including washing machines and car parts, while tightening rules to prevent companies from circumventing the tax. The next round of political talks among the EU co-legislators, the European Council and the European Parliament, is slated for 20 November.

CBAM under international scrutiny

However, resistance to the EU's carbon border tax is growing across the globe.

Canada is trying to negotiate a CBAM exemption with the EU, as the transatlantic partners reinforce closer ties.

The United States is assessing whether the EU's carbon border tax will negatively affect its business operators.

Jodey Arrington, the outgoing US House Budget Committee chairman, joined by ten other members of Congress, wrote to US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, demanding action against EU energy regulations.

“These policies, including the EU’s CBAM, Methane Regulation and Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) discriminate against American producers and suppliers, even as the US maintains some of the highest environmental standards in the world for energy production,” they said.

Meanwhile, the United Kingdom is currently in talks with EU officials to link its carbon market to the EU's own Emissions Trading System (ETS), effectively eyeing a CBAM exemption, according to a document seen by Euronews.

British Financial Secretary to the Treasury Lord Livermore suggested that linking the two carbon markets would prevent British exporters from facing separate carbon border regimes.

“To reduce barriers to trade, the UK and EU are also negotiating a deal to link respective emissions trading schemes, which will create the conditions for mutual CBAM exemptions,” Livermore said in a written parliamentary answer earlier this year.

Russia has an open dispute against the EU's CBAM at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to assess whether the bloc's policy is consistent with WTO rules.

Meanwhile, both Russia and China announced on 3 November that they will join forces at the COP31 against the introduction of unilateral trade barriers.

While Brussels appears to be facing resistance from its global peers, it is also under pressure from its own industries to soften climate costs.

Delays in complying with the methane rules, the ongoing revision of the 2035 ban on new diesel and petrol cars and the EU's ETS are all reflexes of how EU policymakers are rolling back much of what was once hailed as the European Green Deal.

Is the EU losing its climate credibility?

Struggling to keep climate promises at home, Brussels is now heading to the international stage with a somewhat weaker position, bruised by domestic dissent.

The EU risks arriving at COP31 with a weakened negotiating hand, caught between its ambition to present itself as a global climate leader and the political retreat unfolding at home.

Brussels wants the flagship UN climate summit to deliver progress on electrification and moving away from fossil fuels, a decision endorsed at the Santa Marta climate summit, yet EU governments are wrestling with high energy prices, supply concerns and industrial pressure, prompting them to consider expanding domestic refineries.

Environmental activists argue that the EU can't credibly push for a global fossil-fuel phase-out while weakening or delaying elements of its own climate framework.

Sven Harmeling, head of climate at the NGO Climate Action Network Europe, said the EU should help bridge divides at COP31 instead of deepening them.

"The EU cannot ask the rest of the world to deliver while weakening climate action at home or falling short on finance. Leadership in Antalya means doing both: accelerating Europe’s own transition away from fossil fuels and putting its fair share of support on the table internationally," said Harmeling.

The COP31 kicks off on 9 November in Antalya, jointly hosted by Turkey and Australia.

Discreditarea acestora înaintea alegerilor din aprilie 2027 ar putea deschide calea către un al doilea tur de scrutin între candidata de extremă dreapta Marine Le Pen și politicianul de extremă stânga Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Discreditarea candidaților pro-Ucraina din Franța

Glucksmann, copreședintele partidului de centru-stânga Place Publique (PP), este una dintre cele mai puternice voci pro-ucrainene de pe scena politică franceză.

Europarlamentarul social-democrat i-a criticat dur pe liderii europeni pentru că nu fac suficient pentru a ajuta Kievul și a cerut confiscarea activelor rusești imobilizate.

Prin urmare, nu este surprinzător că a devenit una dintre principalele ținte ale dezinformării susținute de Rusia.

În timpul verii, o știre falsă, prezentată ca fiind publicată de publicația franceză de investigații Blast, susținea că partenera lui Glucksmann, Léa Salamé, ar fi încercat să mituiască instituții de presă pentru a publica articole favorabile candidatului. Materialul folosea inclusiv voci generate cu inteligență artificială.

Jurnaliștii de la Blast au negat că ar fi publicat vreodată materialul, în timp ce Glucksmann a denunțat acțiunea drept o operațiune a serviciului de informații militare al Rusiei (GRU).

Atacurile nu s-au oprit aici.

O captură de ecran de pe VT o publicație care se autodefinește drept „presă alternativă” și care amplifică narative pro-Kremlin, arată un articol fals, marcat cu ștampila roșie „FAKE”, publicat pe 29 august 2026. (VT Foreign Policy / Ștampilă: The Kyiv Independent)

VT Foreign Policy, o publicație care se autointitulează „presă alternativă” și amplifică narațiuni favorabile Kremlinului, a publicat pe 29 august un articol fals în care susținea că Glucksmann ar fi contribuit la înființarea unor închisori în care se practica tortura în Georgia, în perioada în care era consilierul președintelui de atunci, Mihail Saakașvili.

Articolul susținea, în continuare, că politicianul francez și-ar fi folosit experiența pentru a înființa structuri similare în Ucraina după Revoluția Euromaidan, în colaborare cu un ofițer militar, Mihailo Drapatîi, prezentat drept actualul comandant-șef al armatei ucrainene.

Publicația cita o singură sursă pentru aceste acuzații: Foundation to Battle Injustice, o organizație-paravan fondată de Evgheni Prigojin, fondatorul grupării Wagner, și sancționată de Uniunea Europeană pentru implicarea în operațiuni de influență ale Rusiei.

Édouard Philippe, fost prim-ministru și actual primar al orașului Le Havre, care s-a întâlnit cu Volodimir Zelenski la Kiev în luna mai, a fost, de asemenea, vizat. Rapoarte false, prezentate ca fiind difuzate de postul de televiziune BFM TV, susțineau că acesta ar suferi de demență.

Tactici similare au fost folosite pentru a răspândi afirmația falsă potrivit căreia Gabriel Attal, fost prim-ministru în timpul mandatului lui Macron, ar fi moștenit de la tatăl său un imperiu al drogurilor.

Campaniile au încercat, de asemenea, să exploateze tensiunile interne din Franța. Materiale false identificate de Bot Blocker pe platforma X susțineau, pe de o parte, că Attal ar sprijini recentul val de proteste studențești și, pe de altă parte, că politicianul ar fi acuzat Rusia de organizarea acestora.

Experții care monitorizează dezinformarea afirmă că metodele folosite și intențiile aparente indică în mod clar implicarea Rusiei.

O captură de ecran care prezintă nouă videoclipuri false, realizate astfel încât să pară reportaje ale unor instituții de presă franceze, printre care BFM, DW, France 24, Le Figaro TV, Le Monde, Le Parisien, Libération și RFI. Acestea răspândesc informații false despre politicianul francez Gabriel Attal și revoltele din școlile din Franța, potrivit inițiativei Bot Blocker. (sursa foto: Bot Blocker/X)

În interiorul mașinăriei de dezinformare a Rusiei

Două campanii notorii asociate Rusiei au vizat alegerile din Franța.

Matryoshka, care distribuie zilnic aproximativ o duzină de materiale false, prezentate ca provenind de la instituții de presă consacrate sau de la experți, este cea mai prolifică dintre acestea, potrivit lui Chine Labbé, vicepreședintă pentru parteneriate și redactor-șef pentru Europa la NewsGuard.

„Până la jumătatea lunii octombrie 2026, număraserăm 89 de materiale false produse de Matryoshka care vizau candidații la alegerile prezidențiale din Franța.”

Cealaltă este Storm-1516, o campanie mai sofisticată, asociată GRU, care utilizează inteligența artificială generativă pentru a crea site-uri întregi.

„Din această vară, am identificat șapte afirmații provenite din această operațiune care vizau candidați francezi, dintre care trei imitau instituții de presă reale”, a declarat Labbé pentru Kyiv Independent.

Potrivit Viginum, materialele false care i-au vizat pe Philippe și Glucksmann în timpul verii au fost produse în cadrul operațiunii Storm-1516.

Aceeași operațiune s-a aflat și în spatele unor materiale false mai recente, prezentate ca fiind publicate de site-ul francez de știri de mediu Reporterre, care susțineau că Glucksmann ar fi cheltuit peste două milioane de euro (2,2 milioane de dolari) pentru zboruri cu avioane private, potrivit organizației independente Gnida Project.

Captură de ecran care prezintă un articol publicat pe 10 octombrie 2026 de un site care se dă drept publicația franceză de știri de mediu Reporterre și care susține în mod fals că Raphaël Glucksmann a cheltuit peste două milioane de euro (2,2 milioane de dolari) pe zboruri cu avioane private. The 20-member cleaning team has created the largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean.

With the longest coastline of any country on the Mediterranean, Greece is blessed with sandy beaches, rocky coves and idyllic islands. But it also faces a rubbish problem – especially on inaccessible shores.

That's where the Typhoon comes in, a 72-metre-long vessel dedicated to cleaning up the Greek coastline. Every day, its 20-member cleaning crew gathers, sorts and documents between 500-1,000 kilograms of waste.

Over the past seven years, the Typhoon Project has completed over 10,000 clean up operations, retrieving 1,140 tonnes of trash – enough to fill around 22 Olympic-sized swimming pools or 1,160 large shipping containers – from remote shores that are not connected to the roads or businesses.

In most cases, it is not litter left by swimmers on the beach, but waste carried there by sea currents.

That is how a beer can with an advert in Spanish for a World Cup from the 1990s ended up on the islet, Patroklos. It lies in the Saronic Gulf, around 65 nautical miles from Athens.

The programme, which began in July 2019, is an initiative of the Public Benefit Foundation 'Athanassios C. Laskaridis'. By February 2023 the first cycle of clean-ups of the island and most of the mainland coastline had been completed.

'The largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean'

Accessing the shores on five inflatable boats, the team gathers waste and takes it on board the ship. But their work does not end there. Besides sorting and transporting the waste to be recycled in the appropriate facilities, there is also the recording and analysis of the data, which is just as important.

"One part of the project is collecting the waste, but the second is collecting the data. We carry out detailed recording of all the waste. We know exactly what quantity there is, how many kilos, how many items from each beach. At the moment we have the largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean, and we are developing it every day," Thanasis Besios, manager of the Typhoon Project, tells Euronews.

The Public Benefit Foundation 'Athanassios C. Laskaridis' started its activities around nine years ago and focuses on three main pillars: protecting the environment, and especially the sea, supporting micro-entrepreneurship and making donations to third parties for the common good.

After seven years of activity in Greek waters, the Typhoon Project's tally is as impressive as it is discouraging.

"With the Typhoon we have collected more than 1,140 tonnes of waste. To help people picture it in their minds, we are talking about 22 Olympic-size swimming pools or around 1160 large containers," notes Peggy Xirotagarou, Executive Director at the Public Benefit Foundation 'Athanassios C. Laskaridis'.

'A large proportion of the waste comes from inland'

But pollution is not a problem that affects only the sea. In many places across the country, uncontrolled, illegal landfills are still operating.

"By observing the waste we were finding on the shores, we realised that a large proportion came from inland. So, in 2024, we created a new programme, called Cyclone. It involves large-scale clean-ups in lakes, rivers and archaeological sites. We have created three large teams in different parts of Greece, where every day we collect more than 1,000 kilos of waste," says Peggy Xirotagarou.

The Typhoon Project cooperates with the Laboratory of Marine Geology and Physical Oceanography of the Department of Geology at the University of Patras to study benthic waste in the Saronic and Thermaic Gulfs, and with the Marine Remote Sensing Research Group of the University of the Aegean to locate and map plastics using modern technology.

It also organises activities with the schools on the islands it visits.

"In every place we visit, we have a holistic approach. Our work is not limited to clean-ups. There are educational programmes that we have designed and run. So in every place we go we also bring the schools in. We go into the classrooms and take the children to the beaches to raise their awareness. Because that is the ultimate goal. For them to become responsible citizens and for this reckless use of single-use plastics to stop," Peggy Xirotagarou tells Euronews.

Essentially a companion piece to McDonagh's debut 'In Bruges', 'Wild Horse Nine' can feel like familiar ground. However, John Malkovich makes every acerbic, funny and at times surprisingly moving line of dialogue a joy to watch, and he's a shoo-in for Best Actor at next year's Oscars.

At this point, it wouldn't be a Martin McDonagh joint without two lonely and dysfunctional souls seeking a warped connection in a world that seems hellbent on imperilling the possibility of redemption.

For his latest black comedy, Wild Horse Nine, the British-Irish writer-director harks back to his feature debut In Bruges - except it's out with two bickering hitmen in Belgium and in with a squabbling pair of CIA operatives on Easter Island prior to the 1973 Chilean coup.

Taking a break from disrupting democracy, seasoned and increasingly forgetful agent Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell), who doesn't mind killing a man while eating a burger, are on holiday. Sort of. The odd couple plan to take in the sights of Rapa Nui, visit the giant stone heads – sorry, Moai - and verbally piss off two pro-Salvador Allende students (Mariana di Girolamo, Ailín Salas) who they keep bumping into.

But everything is not as it seems. Despite his Memento-style notes, Chris' cognitive decline has led him to forget that the trip is also his last hurrah. Not only does he have a bad case of oversharing and wrestles with existential malaise regarding the regimes he's toppled (with a side helping of Catholic guilt), he also riddled with cancer. With not long left, Chris previously asked Lee to Of Mice And Men him on the trip.

He's forgotten that detail, but not his wish to work on his memoir, which he dictates into a tape recorder. These tapes are a source of great discomfort for the pair's boss, chief spook MJ (Steve Buscemi), who fears Chris' indiscretions and confessions - especially "the Dallas parts" which could reveal Chris' role in JFK's assassination - may jeopardise the agency...

While not deviating from his established playbook, Wild Horse Nine feels like a satisfying Best Of compilation from McDonagh, as he merges the narrative framework of In Bruges with Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri 's adoration for the F-bomb, a cheeky Tom Waits cameo (à la Seven Psychopaths), and the more quietly moving qualities at the heart of The Banshees of Inisherin. If that all sounds like your bag, there's a great time to be had.

When the balancing act works, the filmmaker's signature acerbic wit and beloved themes surrounding salvation and unavoidability of death coalesce into a bittersweet whole. When it faulters, his script can feel like a self-indulgent succession of showboating monologues and non-sequitur-filled tangents – a niggle which has resulted in past accusations of narrative bittiness and smugness of tone.

For the most part though, McDonagh pulls it off and plays to his strengths – loading the crackling tirades with some depth. For instance, a breakfast speech explaining why "gay countries" produce better cheeses than the US illicits laughter but also directly feeds into an initially promising commentary on the historic ills of American interventionism - and ongoing horrors of US foreign policy.

Frustratingly, more could have been accomplished here considering the politically charged backdrop, and the female characters do stand out for being underused. It's a pity, as Mariana di Girolamo shines as Monica in the little screentime she is given. She is essentially relegated to being the wide-eyed embodiment of Chris' long-lost optimism, and had she been given more to do, character dynamics could have been amplified and McDonagh could have bolstered his teased critical strands. While the last act hints at transformation before a tough battle ahead, a trick was missed.

Ultimately, enjoyment rests on the double-act chemistry between the leads, which is there in spades and largely rests on Malkovich's capable shoulders. After years of forgettable bit-part roles, the veteran actor is firing on all cylinders and delivers his best performance since Being John Malkovich. Or maybe since his villainous turn as Pascal Sauvage in Johnny English, which is a performance for the ages, and we won’t hear another word about it.

Whether he’s admitting to caring more about the Chilean moths than the people of Chile, irascibly lashing out at whoever happens to be in his vicinity, or musing on why there aren’t more songs about suicidal birds, Malkovich savours every line of dialogue. His trademark elocution suits McDonagh’s prose to a T – especially when he's repeatedly enunciating the word “cahoots”.

What a wonderful word... Did you know it was originally derived from the French 'cahute', meaning a small shack, evoking the image of huddled schemers. Who's to say whether that's gospel, but as Tom Waits once said, "Most people don't care if you're telling them the truth or if you're telling them a lie, as long as they're entertained by it".

Oh god, it's gone all McDonagh with a wordy digression. Back to John...

The way Malkovich manages to simultaneously dip his toes into eccentric, amoral, melancholic and soulful terrains creates pessimistic poetry that his hard to resist. The actor already bagged the Volpi Cup for Best Actor in Venice, where the film premiered this year, and on the strength of this performance he's a shoo-in for Oscar glory next year.

Not hurting those odds is the fact that his last Oscar nomination was in 1993 for In The Line Of Fire – in which he played the unnamed killer attempting to assassinate the President of the United States. The Academy loves a comeback story; and who doesn't love a decent bit of movie-echoing symmetry masquerading as coincidence?

So, familiar ground though Wild Horse Nine may be, there's every chance you'll be hearing a lot more about this sardonic and occasionally moving yarn come awards season.

As Türkiye prepares to host the UN climate summit, one critic describes the country's climate targets and policies as “critically insufficient”.

Row after row of solar panels stretches across a vast landscape in the central Turkish province of Konya, turning sunlight into electricity – and helping Türkiye, the host of the upcoming UN climate summit, spotlight its efforts to expand renewable energy.

Still, advocates for robust action on climate change say Türkiye's cleaner energy ambitions stand in sharp contrast to its continued reliance on coal.

Campaigners also argue the country lacks concrete plans to transition away from fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal, which when burned release greenhouse gases that heat the planet.

Türkiye’s Energy Ministry says coal remained the country’s largest source of electricity last year, accounting for 33 per cent of generation. But it stressed that the share of solar and wind in electricity generation stood at nearly 23 per cent.

Türkiye has one of Europe's largest solar farms

Operational since 2023, it generates enough electricity each year to meet about 0.7 per cent of the country’s power demand, according to plant director Burak Dogru.

“We prevent approximately 1.75 million metric tons of carbon emissions every year,” Dogru told The Associated Press – evidence, he says, of how Türkiye has been directing its economy and energy sector toward cleaner energy sources.

Türkiye’s total greenhouse gas emissions in 2024, the last year for which data is available, reached 584.5 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute.

Duygu Kutluay, a campaigner with the Beyond Fossil Fuels advocacy group, said Türkiye has made plans for a major push in renewable energy.

“But these plans contain neither a roadmap for a coal phase-out, nor any planning for a phase-out of other fossil fuels, including gas,” Kutluay cautioned, adding that this is "not compatible” with Türkiye's pledge to reach net-zero emissions by 2053.

Türkiye is also looking to nuclear power to reduce its energy dependence. The country’s first plant is under construction on the Mediterranean coast, with plans for additional reactors still under consideration.

Concerns and criticism rise ahead of the COP31 summit

Some 265 kilometres away from Konya, the 9-20 November summit in the Mediterranean city of Antalya will bring together tens of thousands of delegates, world leaders, business and civil society representatives for discussions on implementing climate goals.

The summit – officially, the Conference of the Parties, or COP31 – comes against a backdrop of deepening concerns over energy security and the Iran war, which has led to a rise in gas and oil prices and sent countries scrambling to meet energy needs.

Many experts have recently argued that a key mission – combating climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions – has been failing.

The United States, the world’s richest nation and second-biggest carbon polluter after China, will again be absent from the summit, after US President Donald Trump withdrew the US from global climate negotiations.

And the last two summits have ended with little agreement on how to reduce emissions, the final texts not even mentioning fossil fuels.

Türkiye’s environment and climate change minister, Murat Kurum, who will preside over the summit, has said he wants COP31 to focus on turning climate commitments into action rather than new targets.

To that aim, Türkiye will push a “climate implementation bridge”, an initiative to help countries turn climate pledges into action by connecting them with financing, technology and other support.

“Today, the world is not merely waiting for new decisions," Kurum said while presenting summit priorities earlier this year. "What the world wants is to see past decisions put into practice.”

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has insisted his country is committed to environmental protection and combating climate change, and first lady Emine Erdogan has championed a “zero waste” campaign to encourage recycling and a more responsible use of resources.

But shortly afterward, plans emerged to expand another coal-fired power plant in Canakkale, in the country's northwest.

Like other Mediterranean nations, Türkiye faces mounting risks from heatwaves, drought, water scarcity, wildfires and flooding. Last month, rains described as the heaviest in more than 80 years caused severe floods in Istanbul, Türkiye’s largest city, and left eight people dead.

Türkiye was announced as the host of COP31 following a tug-of-war with Australia, which also wanted to host the summit. As a compromise, Australia has been leading consultations to help set the summit's agenda and will be in charge of summit discussions.

But UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell defended the choice, saying in February that a COP host country’s status on fossil fuels does not determine the success or failure of a summit.

The Indian state is encouraging visitors to discover ayurveda on their next visit, and to also come for Onam, a traditional harvest festival in September.

The Kettuvallam, a traditional houseboat, has long been a symbol of tourism in Kerala, with many visitors coming to the Indian state primarily to explore the backwaters.

But that’s certainly not the only reason to visit, with the destination offering up ayurvedic-led wellness, home stays with locals, and cultural festivals.

“Kerala is a destination for all. If your family came to Kerala and each came with different interests, we can offer something for all of them,” P.C. Vishnunadh, Minister for Tourism and Culture for the Government of Kerala, told Euronews Travel at World Travel Market in London.

“You might be coming to see the backwaters, but you can also experience the forest, the beach, our culture, our culinary offering, everything is here.”

The home of ayurveda

Kerala’s tourism board is encouraging visitors to experience its ayurveda offering in 2027 and beyond.

If you’re not familiar with ayurveda, the alternative medicine system goes far beyond just massages, with special diets, meditation and other therapies, and is something that has been practiced in India for thousands of years.

“If you are coming to an ayurvedic resort, the doctors will assess your physical situation and come up with a complete treatment plan,” Vishnunadh added.

“It’s wellness, but it’s not just massage, we can offer treatments based on thousands of years of knowledge.”

Wellness retreats have become hugely popular in recent years, and travellers are increasingly looking for new and interesting experiences in that realm.

Tourism that benefits locals

Another big trend in travel is looking at how tourism can benefit local communities.

Kerala is leaning into this by working together with locals who want to offer home stays, giving them subsidies and other forms of assistance such as training.

“Hotels and resorts are owned by big corporations, whereas home stays are operated by our local people,” Vishnunadh noted.

“Local village people who are offering one or two rooms within their house will benefit from steady employment, but they are also becoming part of our tourism network.”

While it’s not ready yet, the tourism board plans to launch a directory of these home stays to make it easier for tourists to book a room.

Introducing Onam to the world

Kerala Tourism is also looking to promote Onam, a traditional harvest festival, to foreign tourists for the first time.

Taking place over the course of 10 days, the dates of Onam are based on the Malayalam calendar. The festival begins during the month of Chingam, which typically falls between August and September. In 2027, it will begin on 12 September.

The festival is a riot of colours, and begins with the Athachamayam parade where elephants march alongside floats that depict scenes from historical and mythological tales.

You’ll also see dancers painted to look like tigers completing traditional dances, and the season is also associated with snake boat races that see hundreds of people compete on the Pampa River.

For foodies, you won’t want to miss the Onam sadya, or feast. Unsurprisingly for a harvest festival, the feast features plenty of seasonal vegetables.

Served on plantain leaves, there are traditionally nine courses featuring curries, soups, dal and traditional desserts.

EU countries lose nearly €60bn a year to corporate profit shifting, the Tax Justice Network estimates. It links about €8bn of those losses to the UK and its tax haven network, even as the UK itself ranks among the countries that lose the most worldwide.

EU countries lose an estimated €59.3bn a year in tax revenue as multinational companies shift profits across borders, according to the Tax Justice Network. The organisation links about €8bn of these losses to the UK and its Overseas Territories and Crown Dependencies, equivalent to 13.6% of the EU total.

The UK and these jurisdictions also account for more than 30% of the global corporate tax abuse risk measured by the organisation’s Corporate Tax Haven Index.

Profit shifting can happen when companies record profits in lower-tax jurisdictions rather than where the underlying business activity takes place. This can involve payments between companies within the same group, such as interest or royalties, which reduce taxable profits in higher-tax countries.

The OECD says most such schemes are not illegal, although some are. It says these practices undermine the fairness of tax systems and cost governments an estimated $100bn to $240bn (€89bn to €214bn) a year, equivalent to 4% to 10% of global corporate income tax revenue.

Which EU countries lose the most tax revenue?

The Tax Justice Network published its analysis alongside the 5 November update to its Corporate Tax Haven Index. The country figures are for 2022 and cover losses linked to multinational companies rather than individuals.

France leads the list with an estimated loss of €13.1bn in 2022, the latest year for which data are available, followed by Germany at €11.8bn. Together, they account for €24.9bn, or 42% of the EU total.

The estimated annual tax loss exceeds €4bn in Spain (€4.8bn), Poland (€4.7bn) and Belgium (€4.1bn).

The loss is also more than €3bn in Italy (€3.6bn), the Netherlands (€3.5bn) and Luxembourg (€3.2bn).

It exceeds €1bn in Ireland (€2.2bn), Sweden (€1.6bn) and Austria (€1.1bn). The loss is below €1bn in all other EU countries.

Lithuania (€59mn), Malta (€61mn), Latvia (€68mn), Estonia (€73mn) and Croatia (€75mn) have the lowest estimated tax losses, all below €100mn.

How much of the EU’s tax loss is linked to UK tax havens?

The Tax Justice Network says this is the first time it has estimated how much each EU country loses through corporate profit shifting linked to the UK’s network of tax havens. It puts the combined loss at about €8bn.

France and Germany have the largest estimated losses linked to the UK network. In France, the network is linked to €2.8bn, or 21.3% of the country’s estimated losses from corporate profit shifting. That is the highest share in the EU. In Germany, the equivalent figures are €1.4bn and 11.9%.

The estimated losses linked to the UK network are €570mn for Luxembourg, €475mn for Spain, €438mn each for Poland and Italy, and €415mn for Belgium.

UK network linked to a third of global corporate tax abuse risk

The Corporate Tax Haven Index ranks jurisdictions by the risk that their tax rules and financial activity enable multinational corporations to reduce the tax they pay elsewhere. It combines an assessment of laws and regulations with the scale of foreign direct investment entering and leaving each jurisdiction.

Four British jurisdictions rank in the top 10 of the index. The British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands and Bermuda rank first, second and third, while Jersey ranks eighth. Two more British jurisdictions, Guernsey and the Isle of Man, rank in the top 20, with the UK in 19th place.

Together, the UK and these six jurisdictions account for 31% of the global corporate tax abuse risk identified by the index.

The index also includes Gibraltar, Anguilla, the Turks and Caicos Islands and Montserrat. Including these four British Overseas Territories brings the combined share to 33.3%.

The Crown Dependencies set their own tax rules, and tax policy in the British Overseas Territories is generally decided locally. The UK retains powers to intervene in the territories, although it rarely legislates on their domestic affairs.

Euronews Business contacted HM Treasury for comment on the findings.

The Tax Justice Network also ranks the UK among the countries with the largest losses from corporate profit shifting. It estimates that the UK itself loses £12.8bn (€14.7bn) a year as multinationals shift profits to tax havens around the world. This is an annual average for 2018 to 2022.

“The Corporate Tax Haven Index continues to demonstrate the UK’s oversized role in the landscape of global corporate tax abuse risk. The UK and EU stand to gain the most from the changes the UN tax convention aims to deliver, but they remain opposed to them,” Moran Harari, the Tax Justice Network’s index lead, said in the release.

“They continue to hold on to the discredited and unscientific fantasy of ‘tax competition’, but our findings today again confirm that this only leads to a race to the bottom with no winners.”

The organisation said that despite years of international efforts to tackle corporate tax abuse through the OECD, many countries still fail to require companies to disclose the basic information tax authorities need to detect it.

Global losses rise when wealthy individuals are included

When wealthy individuals are included, the estimated tax loss is much larger. The State of Tax Justice 2024 report puts global losses at €416bn ($492bn) a year. This covers both profit shifting by multinational corporations and tax evasion involving undeclared offshore wealth held by wealthy individuals. Companies account for about 71% of the total.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday urged Latin American leaders to send help "as soon as possible" to save his country's power grid from relentless Russian attacks.

Speaking at a summt in Madrid, Zelenskyy said every power plant in Ukraine has been damaged "in one way or another by attacks".

The Ukrainian leader asked for international cooperation to help rebuild and repair its energy system.

"We need equipment that works with our power grid and we need it fast. So please support directly to have connections with your companies, with your productions and get these supplies to Ukraine as quick as possible," Zelenskyy said at the 30th Ibero-American summit.

The summit brought together a 22-nation group of mainly Latin American Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries.

Those attending included Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, Guatemalan President Bernardo Arevalo, Honduran President Nasry Asfura, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and European Council President Antonio Costa.

"Since the start of the war, Ukraine has sought integration and the right kind of communication about this war with countries on the African continent and in Latin America," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that it is the first time Ukraine is represented at the summit.

"We need the diplomatic support of these countries. Every day, every month, and every year, relevant issues are raised at the UN General Assembly, and we are getting more and more votes from Latin America," he added.

Ukraine faces another difficult winter

Speaking at the summit, Zelenskyy called on leaders across the region to speak out against what he described as Russian "mass killings" that it carries out throughbombings and drones.

The Ukrainian president, who thanked Spain for its continued support, set out the urgent need for technical equipment, such as transformers, power cables, electronic equipment and diesel and gas generators to maintain the country's infrastructure.
